 Do students prefer daylight saving time or standard time? 
 By Emily Jones 
 Nov 16, 2026 
 Views: 0 
 Daylight saving time (DST) came to an end on Nov. 1, 2026. This change affects most of the United States with the exception of Hawaii (Hawaii Standard Time, HST), most of Arizona (Mountain Standard Time, MST, excluding the Navajo Nation), and U.S. territories such as Guam, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
 Daylight saving time moves the clocks one hour forward to shift an hour of daylight from early morning to the evening due to where we are located on the globe, and the earth’s axial tilt as it orbits the sun. We are currently in standard time, the time system used from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November. Standard Time is the baseline time zone for different regions (PST, CST, EST, etc.), which aligns more closely with the sun’s position in the sky. When the time is adjusted slightly, there are earlier sunrises and earlier sunsets.
 DST – A view of the PLNU track and tennis court at sunset. Photo by Emily Jones/The Point. 
 In an AP-NORC poll published on Oct. 30, 2025, 47% of Americans were opposed to changing their clocks twice a year, 12% were in favor and 40% were neutral. More than half of the adults – 56% – preferred to make DST the permanent choice when having to choose between the two. On July 14, 2026, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act , which would make DST the permanent standard time. However, the Senate has not passed the bill. 
 In the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine , studies found that later sunrises and sunsets do not naturally align with our natural circadian rhythm, and are associated with several long-term health implications such as an increase in strokes, heart attacks, diabetes, obesity and cancer during the week following the time change.
 With this circadian rhythm disruption, it can cause short-term fatigue. For many college students, the changing of times affects motivation, sleep schedules and seems to have more negative effects than positive.
 “I’m personally not a fan of daylight saving time because as a student, it can throw off our routines, affect our sleep and proves that changing the clock doesn’t mean we’re saving time,” James Wagner, a fourth-year business major, said. “Most activities I do are better to be done in the daytime, so it just seems to me that daylight saving is more of a negative and unnecessary thing.”
 Quincy McGinnis, a third-year math major from Arizona, said that she finds the time change “unusual.”
 “We don’t do daylight saving, so I get thrown off by the time change every year,” McGinnis said. “It doesn’t make sense at all when the sun goes down and what time I start to get tired anymore.”
 Katie Bushelman, a third-year child and adolescent development major, echoed McGinnis.
 “I grew up in Arizona my whole life, so coming to college was the first time I experienced the time change,” Bushelman said. “It makes me want to fall asleep at 8:30 [p.m.] every night.”
 One positive of the time change is that out-of-state students with a time difference between states are able to communicate easier with their family.
 “The time difference is only two hours now between San Diego and home so it’s easier to communicate with my family back home,” Savannah Hubbard, third-year biology major, said. Hubbard is from Kauai, Hawaii, and said that despite this, she still prefers HST since they don’t have daylight saving time.
 “It’s such a foreign concept to me, and I never had to deal with it until college,” Hubbard said.
 Keiilani Binsol, third-year nursing major, remained neutral, and said the effects she experiences are not major for either time change. 
 “I honestly do not have a preference for either. The only differences I feel are the hour of sleep we gained and the sun setting earlier,” Binsol said.
 For myself, I would prefer not to participate in daylight saving. I have dealt with symptoms of fatigue when the days are shorter. I find myself struggling to stay within a consistent sleep schedule. However, there are steps I take to combat these issues.
 Something I do when I begin feeling drowsy is go on a run or walk – typically around 7 p.m. Getting oxygen pumping and adrenaline rushing helps to make you feel more alert and clear brain fog. Having bright overhead lights can help to suppress melatonin production, which for most on campus living spaces there are bright lights. Students can also optimize that 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. gap to maximize social interaction or activities to get a sense of satisfaction or productivity even when the sun has set.
 Students do not have to passively accept the slump that comes with daylight saving time. By treating each day with intentionality, students can make the most of the day and reclaim energy.
